Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Some friends are having a conversation about how boring things have gotten ... in the middle of a comically dramatic / dangerous / or otherwise intense scene .
content:
The train had been going downhill for seven minutes, which was six minutes longer than anyone had expected.

“Brakes are gone!” shouted the conductor, staggering through the carriage as it lurched around a bend. “Everybody stay calm!”

A suitcase flew past his head. Somewhere behind them, a child cheered.

Maya tightened her grip on the seat. Across from her, Ben peered out the window at the pine trees streaking by.

“You know what?” he said. “I was just saying things had gotten boring.”

Priya gave him a look. “You said *our weekends* had gotten boring.”

“Same thing, really.”

The train clattered over a bridge. The bridge clattered back.

Maya grabbed the overhead rail. “I can’t believe you’re making this about your social calendar.”

“I’m not making it about my social calendar. I’m saying this is the first interesting thing that’s happened to us in months.”

“We’re on a runaway train!”

“Exactly. Very interesting.”

The conductor hurried past again, now carrying a fire extinguisher. “The track splits ahead! If we take the left fork, we’ll go into the old quarry. If we take the right, we’ll go through the tunnel!”

“Which one is safer?” Maya called.

“I don’t know!” he yelled, disappearing into the next carriage.

Ben nodded thoughtfully. “That’s the sort of uncertainty I’ve been missing.”

Priya leaned across the aisle and smacked his arm. “You’ve been missing uncertainty? You ordered the same sandwich every day for three years.”

“It’s a reliable sandwich.”

The train screamed around another corner. A hat sailed through the carriage and landed on Priya’s head. She kept it on.

Maya looked through the window. Ahead, the track divided: one branch curved toward a dark tunnel, the other toward a quarry edged with jagged gray rock.

“Can we pull the emergency brake?” she shouted.

“Already pulled!” the conductor shouted back.

The train did not slow.

“Maybe the emergency brake is more of a suggestion,” Ben said.

“Ben!”

“What? I’m just trying to stay positive.”

Priya stood, bracing herself against the seats. “There’s a lever by that door. It says ‘WHISTLE.’”

“That’s the whistle,” Maya said.

“Then why is it so dramatically labeled?”

Priya yanked it. The train let out a deafening blast. Ahead, a flock of birds burst from the trees. The conductor stuck his head through the doorway.

“Why are you whistling?”

“To alert people!” Priya yelled.

“Who?”

“Anyone who might be able to help!”

The conductor considered this, then vanished again.

Ben watched the tunnel rush closer. “I think we should make a list of things we want to do if we survive.”

Maya stared at him. “You want to make a bucket list right now?”

“Not a whole list. Just one thing each. Something exciting.”

Priya lifted the borrowed hat off her head. “I want to go somewhere with a beach.”

“That’s not exciting,” Ben said.

“I want to go somewhere with a beach where we don’t have to discuss whether it’s exciting.”

“Fair.”

Maya looked at the oncoming tunnel. “I want to have one quiet dinner where nobody says the words ‘bucket list.’”

The train plunged into darkness.

For a few seconds, there was only the shriek of metal and the thunder of wheels. Then the lights flickered back on.

At the far end of the tunnel, a maintenance cart sat on the tracks.

“Oh,” said Ben. “That’s unfortunate.”

The conductor appeared in the doorway, pale as paper. “Everyone brace!”

Maya grabbed Priya’s hand. Priya grabbed Ben’s sleeve. Ben grabbed the seat.

The train hit the cart.

It launched upward, flipped once, and landed—somehow—on a parallel track. The carriages shuddered, slowed, and finally rolled to a stop beside a field of yellow flowers.

Silence settled over the passengers.

Then the child cheered again.

The conductor stumbled into their carriage. “Are you all right?”

Maya let go of Priya’s hand. “I think so.”

Ben looked out at the flowers. “Well. That was certainly different.”

Priya took off the conductor’s hat, which had landed on her head this time. “Next weekend, we’re going to the beach.”

“Quietly,” Maya said.

“Of course,” Ben replied. “Unless something exciting happens.”

Maya pointed at him.

He zipped his lips.

For almost three full seconds, nobody said a word.

Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: The time of Armageddon is soon . All the gods of various pantheons congregate to debate on why their end of the world should happen . While squabbling among each other , a god that was never worshiped speaks its mind .
content:
### The God of Morning

The gods met at the hinge of the world, where the last hour of the old age ticked like a clock with a cracked face.

Below them, the Earth turned beneath storm clouds. The seas had begun to climb their shores. A red star burned in the east. In cities and villages, people looked up from their work and felt—without knowing why—that something was coming.

“Then let it be fire,” said the Thunderer, and lightning coiled around his fingers. “The world should end in a blaze worthy of its beginning.”

“Fire is so brief,” said the Lady of the Deep. “Let the waters take it. They will remember nothing but my name.”

The Lord of the Last Battle struck his spear against the floor. “You would drown a world without giving it a chance to fight? Let the dead rise. Let the living earn their ending.”

Around them, gods argued over ash and ice, famine and flood, trumpets and silence. Each offered a better apocalypse than the last. Each insisted the end belonged to them.

At the edge of the assembly sat a small, gray figure on an uncarved stone.

No one had noticed him arrive.

“Who invited you?” demanded the Thunderer.

“No one,” said the figure.

“Then who are you?”

The figure stood. He wore no crown, carried no weapon, and cast no shadow.

“I am the god of morning.”

The gods laughed. Even the floor seemed to shiver with it.

“Morning?” said the Lady of the Deep. “Who worships morning?”

“No one,” he replied. “Not directly.”

“Then you are no god.”

The gray figure looked down through the crack in the world. Far below, in a village under a bruised sky, a woman was helping an old man carry firewood indoors. In a city, a boy was covering his little sister’s ears against the thunder. A farmer had stopped in the road to move a turtle from the path.

“I have never had a temple,” said the god. “No one has offered me a crown or a sacrifice. People simply wake, and begin again.”

“Begin again?” The Lord of the Last Battle lifted his spear. “The world is ending.”

“Yes,” said the god. “You have all made certain of that.”

The gods fell quiet—not because they agreed, but because the small god had spoken as if they were not the most important beings in the room.

“You are quarreling over whose name will be remembered at the end,” he continued. “But if you end everything, there will be no one left to remember you. No songs. No prayers. No stories. Only the silence you keep promising one another.”

The Thunderer’s lightning dimmed a little.

The god of morning turned toward them. “You don’t want the world to end. You want to be the one who ends it.”

“That is not the same,” said the Lady of the Deep.

“Isn’t it?”

Below, the red star brightened. The seas rose higher. The first thunderclap shook the heavens.

The gods looked at one another. For the first time, they saw not rivals, but witnesses to the same small planet.

“What would you have us do?” asked the Lord of the Last Battle.

The god of morning looked down again. The woman had brought the old man inside. The boy had begun telling his sister a story.

“Let them have the next hour,” he said.

“And if they fail?” asked the Thunderer.

“Then you will still have your endings.”

The gods looked toward the world, where the first wave curled over the harbor wall.

One by one, they lowered their hands.

The Lady of the Deep called her waters back from the shore. The Lord of the Last Battle sent the dead to sleep. The Thunderer closed his fist around the lightning until it became a spark, then let it go.

The red star faded.

On Earth, people waited for the sky to split.

Instead, the rain began.

By dawn, the gods had gone their separate ways. None of them left an offering for the small, gray figure. None asked his name.

They did not need to.

Across the waking world, people opened their doors, looked at one another, and began again.

prompt: Special Division Infantry , Necromancer Class .
content:
**The Necromancer Class**

The army called them the Special Division Infantry. The newspapers called them ghosts.

Mara Venn called them by their names.

She stood in the rain beside the shattered wall, one hand pressed to the earth. Beneath her palm, the battlefield stirred—not with life, but with memory. The dead remembered their boots, their rifles, the orders that had carried them here.

“Only volunteers,” Mara whispered.

The first hand rose from the mud. Then another. Soldiers emerged in torn uniforms, pale as moonlight, each wearing the face they’d worn at the moment of death.

Captain Orrel climbed from the crater, a hole in his chest glowing softly.

“Lieutenant,” he said. “You’re late.”

Mara let out a breath that almost became a laugh. “Traffic.”

Behind her, the living infantry waited in the broken street. The enemy’s armored column was coming. They had no tanks left, no air support, and barely enough ammunition to make a convincing noise.

Orrel looked past her at the approaching lights. “What do you need?”

“Time.”

“Then we’ll give you time.”

The dead formed ranks—not the ragged horde the enemy expected, but a proper infantry line. They remembered their training. They remembered how to cover one another. They remembered the people they had promised to bring home.

When the enemy came through the fog, the dead stood their ground.

Mara fought beside them, directing the living, calling the fallen by name. Every ghost who took a hit broke apart into silver dust. Every one who fell made the line thinner.

But the enemy slowed.

Then stopped.

Then turned back.

At dawn, the battlefield was quiet. The ghosts began to fade, one by one, their duty finally finished.

Orrel was the last to go.

“You did good, Venn,” he said.

“You did the hard part.”

He glanced toward the sunrise. “That’s infantry.”

And then the rain passed through him, and he was gone.

**The Last Bell**

The bell began to ring just as the floodgate broke.

Mara felt the first удар through the iron floor: a deep, shuddering boom from somewhere below. Then came the roar of water rushing into the old pumping station.

She lunged for the red lever.

A boot struck her ribs and sent her skidding across the slick tiles.

“Not that one,” said Venn.

He stood between her and the controls, rainwater running from his coat. In one hand he held a short steel baton. In the other, the brass key to the river gates.

Behind him, through the arched windows, the town’s lights glimmered beneath the storm. The river was already over its banks. If Mara couldn’t open the upper sluice, the lower streets would drown.

“You said you’d help,” she gasped.

“I did help.” Venn nodded toward the broken gate mechanism. “I got us inside.”

Mara pushed herself up on one elbow. Her ribs complained. “There are children in the school.”

“There are always children somewhere.”

He came at her.

Mara rolled aside as the baton cracked against the floor. She swept her wrench at his ankle. He stepped over it and drove a knee into her shoulder. The wrench clattered away.

She stumbled backward into the bank of old control wheels. One spun beneath her hand, making the machinery groan. Venn caught her by the collar and slammed her against the panel.

“Give me the key,” she said.

He smiled. “That’s what I came for.”

His fist hit her cheek. White light burst behind her eyes. She grabbed the front of his coat and pulled him down with her, taking them both to the floor. The brass key skittered away beneath the controls.

They scrambled after it.

{prompt}
prompt: The most beautiful woman in the world
content:
### The Most Beautiful Woman in the World

When the magazine announced its annual search for the most beautiful woman in the world, the judges expected thousands of photographs.

They got millions.

There were actresses beneath studio lights, athletes on podiums, grandmothers in sunlit kitchens, and a girl in a yellow raincoat who had apparently taken a picture of her own reflection in a puddle. The judges argued over cheekbones, smiles, and the exact meaning of *beauty* until their coffee went cold.

At last, they chose a woman named Mara Vale.

Mara had never been photographed professionally. She lived in a little house at the edge of a coastal town, where the wind rattled the windows and the sea brought in more driftwood than visitors. When the magazine’s letter arrived, she read it twice, certain it had been sent by mistake.

Then she took the bus to the city.

The interview was held in a room with white walls and a vase of flowers so perfect they looked artificial. A reporter sat across from her, pen poised.

“How does it feel,” he asked, “to be called the most beautiful woman in the world?”

Mara considered this.

“Like being handed a very expensive vase,” she said. “I’m afraid I’ll drop it.”

The reporter laughed, though she hadn’t meant to be funny.

They asked her to stand beneath the lights. A photographer circled her, adjusting the angle of her chin.

“Could you look happier?” he said.

Mara tried.

“More mysterious.”

She tried that too.

“Now, imagine the person you love most.”

Mara closed her eyes. She pictured her mother, who had taught her to mend a torn sleeve with the patience of a saint. She pictured her brother, who had once walked three miles in a blizzard to bring her a jar of peaches. She pictured the neighbors who left soup on her porch when the flu went through town.

When she opened her eyes, the photographer lowered his camera.

“That’s it,” he said quietly.

The magazine came out a month later. Mara’s face filled the cover. People stopped her in the street. Some asked for photographs; others asked what cream she used, what she ate, how she kept her hair so bright beneath the rain.

She answered honestly. The cream came from a pharmacy. She ate whatever was in the cupboard. Her hair, she suspected, had always been that color.

Still, the attention made her uneasy. Beauty, she discovered, was a room into which everyone wanted to enter, but nobody asked whether you wished to be there.

One afternoon, she found a child sitting on the seawall, crying. The girl had scraped her knee and was holding a broken red balloon. Mara sat beside her and took a clean handkerchief from her pocket.

“Does it hurt?” she asked.

The girl nodded.

“Then we’ll wait a little,” Mara said. “Sometimes hurting needs a moment.”

The child leaned against her shoulder. The wind tugged at the loose strands of Mara’s hair. The balloon slipped from the girl’s hand and rolled down the beach, where the tide carried it away.

A photographer across the street lifted his camera.

Mara saw him and turned her face—not from shame, and not from vanity, but to give the girl a little privacy.

Years later, when the magazine held another contest, they asked Mara to sit on the judging panel. She agreed on one condition: they must accept entries without photographs.

The other judges protested. How could they choose the most beautiful woman in the world without seeing her?

Mara placed a box on the table. Inside were hundreds of letters.

There was one from a nurse who had held a stranger’s hand through the night. One from a farmer who had fed a hungry family before selling his own harvest. One from a girl who wrote that her sister had smiled at her after months of silence.

The judges read until the room grew still.

At sunset, Mara walked home along the shore. The water shone copper and rose. She passed the seawall where the child had once sat, and heard laughter somewhere beyond the dunes.

For a moment, the whole world seemed to hold its breath—not because it was looking at her, but because she was looking at it.

And Mara understood, finally, what the title meant.

The most beautiful woman in the world was not the one everyone wanted to see.

She was the one who made someone else feel seen.

Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Death comes to collect someone and ends up falling in love with them .
content:
### The Last Light

Death arrived at the lighthouse at midnight, soaked to the bone.

Mara Vale opened the door before he could knock. She was seventy-three, thin as a matchstick, and wearing a yellow oilskin coat over her nightgown.

“You’re late,” she said.

Death glanced at the black sea behind him. “The road was difficult.”

“There isn’t a road.”

“Exactly.”

Mara stepped aside. “Come in, then. You’ll catch your death.”

He looked at her.

She smiled. “That was a joke.”

“I know,” he said. “I’m trying to learn them.”

The lighthouse was warm, though the storm rattled every window. A kettle steamed on the stove. A half-mended net lay across the table, and above it a small clock ticked with an uneven, determined sound.

Death took off his coat. He had no idea why. He had no need to be comfortable.

“Tea?” Mara asked.

“I don’t drink.”

“Then you can keep me company while I do.”

She poured a cup and sat. Death remained standing.

“You’ve come for me,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Tonight?”

“Yes.”

She looked toward the lantern room, where the great lamp turned and turned, casting its bright sweep over the water. “I thought I had another week.”

“People often do.”

“Are you always this cheerful?”

“No.”

“Good. I’d hate to think I was getting your special treatment.”

Death studied her. He had met fear in a thousand shapes: anger, bargaining, silence, prayer. Mara seemed to have set hers aside for the moment, like a coat she’d take up again if the weather changed.

“What are you afraid of?” he asked.

She considered. “That the lamp will go out.”

“It won’t.”

“Not tonight?”

“Not tonight.”

She nodded, satisfied. Then she pushed the second cup toward him, though it was empty. “There. Now you’re included.”

Death sat.

For a while, they listened to the storm. Mara told him about the ships she’d guided through fog, and the ones she hadn’t. She spoke of her husband, who had died forty years ago, and of the daughter who’d moved inland and called every Sunday. She spoke, too, of ordinary things: the roof that leaked above the pantry, the neighbor’s goat that had once climbed the lighthouse stairs, the fact that she’d never learned to swim.

“You lived beside the sea and never learned?” Death asked.

“I knew where the sea was. That seemed enough.”

He found himself smiling. It was a strange, small movement, as if some old hinge had loosened.

Mara noticed. “There you are.”

“Where?”

“Underneath all that solemnity.”

“I am not solemn.”

“You’re Death.”

“Those aren’t the same thing.”

“No,” she said. “I suppose they aren’t.”

She stood abruptly and winced. One hand went to her chest.

Death rose with her. “Mara.”

“Just a flutter,” she said, though her face had gone pale. “It happens.”

He could feel the moment approaching. The invisible thread drawing taut. His hand, which had taken kings and children and everyone between, hovered near her shoulder.

“I can make it quick,” he said.

She looked up at him. “I know.”

“I can make it painless.”

“I know.”

The wind battered the lighthouse. The lamp kept turning.

Mara reached for his hand. His fingers were cold, but she folded hers around them as if she were the one offering comfort.

“Will you stay with me?” she asked.

“I’m here.”

“No. I mean after.”

Death had never been asked that. He had always been the last companion, the closed door, the hand that led you to the threshold and no farther.

“I don’t know what happens after,” he said.

“Neither do I.”

Her grip tightened. “Then we’ll be surprised together.”

Something in him broke—not loudly, not all at once. More like ice giving way beneath a careful foot.

He had taken millions. He had never wanted to keep anyone.

“Mara,” he said, and her name sounded different now. Not a task. Not a destination. A name.

Her breath caught. “Is it time?”

“Yes.”

She glanced toward the lantern room. “Let me turn it once more.”

Death nodded.

Together they climbed the spiral stairs. At the top, Mara checked the flame and wiped a thumb over the glass. The light swung out over the waves, brushed the dark horizon, and returned.

“There,” she whispered. “Someone will see it.”

Then her knees gave way.

Death caught her. He held her as gently as he could, though he had never before understood that gentleness might be something other than carefulness.

Mara looked at him, her face peaceful now. “You’ll remember me?”

“I remember everyone,” he said.

“No,” she murmured. “I mean will you miss me?”

The question filled the lantern room. Outside, the sea hurled itself against the rocks.

“Yes,” Death said.

Mara smiled. “Then I’m glad you came.”

Her hand went still in his.

For a moment, Death stayed exactly where he was, holding her while the lighthouse turned its light across the world. Then he rose, carrying her with him—not as a burden, but as someone he had chosen to walk beside.

At the threshold, Mara looked back once at the lamp.

“It’s still burning,” he told her.

“I know.”

And together they stepped into the dark, where, for the first time, Death did not feel alone.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: For as long as you can remember , you can hear background music appropriate to the situation you 're in . While going to the grocery store one day , you hear what sounds like the most generic JRPG battle theme you 've ever heard .
content:
### Random Encounter

I have always heard music.

Not all the time. There are quiet stretches—brushing my teeth, waiting for the kettle, lying awake at three in the morning—but most situations come with a score. School hallways had nervous strings. Rainy days got piano. My first kiss, disappointingly, had a ukulele.

I never told anyone. It seemed like the sort of thing people would want tested.

On Tuesday, I went to the grocery store for coffee, dish soap, and the particular brand of crackers my doctor had called “a reasonable compromise.”

I was comparing two jars of instant coffee when the music began.

A fast, bright melody. Drums like someone enthusiastically tapping a cardboard box. A brass line that sounded as if it had been written by a computer asked to compose “heroic adventure” and given twelve seconds to do it.

The most generic JRPG battle theme I had ever heard.

I looked around.

A child sat in a shopping cart. A woman squeezed avocados. An employee stacked cans of soup. Nobody seemed to notice that an imaginary orchestra had just announced an encounter.

I abandoned the coffee and wandered toward the music.

It got louder in aisle six.

A man in a gray coat was leaning over the checkout counter, red-faced. “It said two for five,” he snapped. “You people put up the sign, then you charge me seven dollars?”

The cashier was young, maybe nineteen. She had her hands folded on the counter and was staring at the register as if it might open up and swallow her.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I can ask my manager to check.”

“You should check before you charge people.”

The battle theme looped. A little cymbal crash marked the end of the phrase.

I stood with my basket of coffee, soap, and medically approved crackers. I could have kept walking. I was very good at keeping walking. I had built an entire adult life out of not making other people’s difficult moments more difficult.

The music played on.

In my head, a menu appeared.

**FIGHT**  
**ITEM**  
**RUN**

There was no **RUN** option that didn’t involve leaving the cashier alone with him.

I set my basket down.

“Hey,” I said.

The man turned. “What?”

“I think she said she’d get the manager.”

He looked me up and down, as though checking whether I was worth being angry at. “This doesn’t concern you.”

“No,” I said. My voice came out thinner than I’d hoped. “But she’s trying to help.”

The music hit a dramatic flourish. It was the sort of flourish that suggested the hero had successfully selected **DEFEND**.

The man’s face tightened. For a second, I thought he might shout at me instead. Then his shoulders dropped, just a little.

“I’m trying to feed my dad,” he said. “They keep changing the prices. Every week, something costs more.”

The cashier looked up. “I can check the sign,” she said. “I really can.”

He looked at her, then at the floor. “Fine. Check it.”

She called her manager. The three of us waited while the store’s overhead speakers played a gentle song about summer, a completely different piece of music from the one in my head.

The manager came over and checked the shelf. The sign was wrong. The man had been right.

“I’m sorry,” the cashier said, though she had nothing to apologize for.

The man rubbed his forehead. “I shouldn’t have yelled.”

“No,” I said, then worried that I’d said it too quickly. “But you can start over.”

He looked at me. The battle theme softened, losing its drums.

He turned to the cashier. “I’m sorry I yelled at you.”

“Thank you,” she said.

The manager fixed the price. The man paid. I picked up my basket. No one clapped. No glowing chest appeared. The cashier gave me a tired smile, and the man left with his groceries.

As I rolled toward the coffee aisle, the music changed.

Not a victory fanfare. Not quite.

Just a modest little tune, warm and unhurried, like the map after the monsters are gone.

I bought the cheaper coffee. It was terrible.

But on the way home, I found myself humming the battle theme—and, for once, it didn’t sound generic at all.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: You have been kidnapped by a cult that holds a famous novel as its sacred text . The cult 's leader explains what lies in store for you .
content:
They took me from the ferry terminal because I was carrying a copy of *Moby-Dick*.

Not my copy. Theirs.

It was swollen with damp and patched with strips of sailcloth, its pages crowded with notes in a cramped blue hand. I’d found it on a bench and picked it up to see if someone had left a name inside. Then the people in gray coats closed around me.

By the time I woke, I was aboard a ship.

The cabin smelled of salt, lamp oil, and old wood. My wrists were tied behind me. Through the round porthole, the harbor lights trembled on black water.

The man who entered wore a captain’s coat. He was tall and neatly bearded, with a gold tooth that flashed when he smiled.

“I’m Elias Vale,” he said. “You may call me Captain.”

“Where am I?”

“On the *Pequod*.”

I looked at the porthole. “That ship sank.”

“Not this one.” He sat across from me and placed the patched novel on the table. “This is the *Miriam*. But names are only the first layer of a thing.”

I tested the knots at my wrists. “You kidnapped me because I picked up a book?”

“Because you read the opening line aloud.”

I remembered doing it. *Call me Ishmael.* Just a murmur to myself, in the ferry terminal.

Vale leaned forward. “The book is not a story. It is an account of what must happen. It tells us the shape of the world, and what happens to those who sail against it.”

“And what happens to me?”

His smile softened, almost kindly. “You are Ishmael.”

“I’m not.”

“You said the words.”

“That doesn’t make me a character.”

“To us, it does.” He tapped the cover. “At dawn, we leave the harbor. We’ll follow the old whaling route north. At the end, the captain will meet the great white thing. The crew will go down with him.”

“And me?”

“You will survive. The book says so.”

He said it as if he were offering me a seat in a lifeboat.

I stared at him. “You’re planning to kill everyone?”

“Not kill. Fulfill.”

He rose and walked to the door. “You’ll be kept below until the final day. Then you’ll witness the end and carry the account back to shore.”

“You want me to tell people you drowned your followers because a novel told you to?”

“I want you to tell them what happened.”

He left me with the book.

For a while I did nothing but listen to the ship creak. Then I dragged the book toward me with my bound hands and flipped through it. The blue handwriting filled every margin. Some notes were prayers. Others were instructions: *Keep the fire low. Keep the boat secured. Do not let the crew question the captain.*

On the last page, someone had written: *Ishmael survives by the coffin.*

A shadow moved beneath the door.

“Is someone there?” I whispered.

The shadow stayed still.

“The book doesn’t say Ishmael survives because he’s chosen,” I said. “He survives because he’s lucky. There’s a coffin that turns into a lifebuoy.”

The shadow shifted.

“Who are you?” I asked.

“Ruth,” a girl’s voice whispered. “I’m supposed to bring you food.”

“Do you believe him?”

A pause. Then: “I believe he believes it.”

I leaned closer to the door. “The captain in the book doesn’t save the crew. He kills them. Is that what you signed up for?”

“I signed up to sail.”

“And if he says the ending is fixed?”

The lock clicked.

Ruth slipped inside, carrying a tin cup. She was young, with a shaved head and a strip of blue cloth tied around her wrist. She had a key in her palm.

“He says the sea has already decided,” she whispered.

“Does the sea know about the engine?”

She blinked.

I nodded toward the deck. “A ship doesn’t have to meet a whale. It can meet a harbor patrol. Or a reef. Or a broken engine.”

Ruth looked at the open book. “He says doubt is how the whale speaks.”

“Then let him hear it.”

She untied my hands.

We went up through the passageway together. Voices drifted from the deck: Vale addressing his crew, telling them they had been chosen to take part in something eternal. Beyond the cabin door, the harbor glowed with morning lights. The ship’s engine throbbed beneath our feet.

Ruth led me to the engine room. She knew where the fuel shutoff was. I knew enough about boats to understand that pulling it would stop us from leaving—but not enough to know whether Vale had a backup plan.

We pulled it anyway.

The engine coughed, shuddered, and went quiet.

A bell rang above us. Someone shouted. Then Vale’s voice cut through the confusion.

“Hold your stations!”

Ruth and I ran for the gangway. The crew had gathered on deck, looking from the dark engine room to their captain. Vale stood at the bow, one hand on the rail.

“The book has already told us how this ends,” he called.

“No,” Ruth said.

It wasn’t loud, but the silence carried it.

Vale’s expression changed. For the first time, he looked less like a captain than a man who had misplaced his place in a story.

I reached the gangway. No one stopped me. One by one, the crew lowered their eyes, then stepped away from the ropes.

Vale remained at the bow as the harbor patrol boat approached, its blue lights flickering across the water.

When I reached shore, I looked back. The *Miriam* sat dark and still in the harbor. Vale hadn’t moved. He was staring out to sea, waiting, perhaps, for the white thing to appear.

I kept the book.

The last page was still marked in blue: *Ishmael survives by the coffin.*

I crossed out *by the coffin* and wrote beneath it: *by getting off the ship.*

content:
### The Human Exhibit

At the Museum of Inhabited Worlds, the new exhibit was labeled **TERRESTRIAL HUMANS**.

The label had taken six months to agree upon.

The Venn, who lived beneath a global ocean, had proposed: *A violent surface species that cooperates in order to become more violent.*

The Tath, whose bodies grew in branching colonies, preferred: *A social organism that mistakes its temporary clusters for individuals.*

The scholars of Lume had offered the most concise description: *A mammal with tools.*

This was rejected as too vague. The Lume had tools. So did the Venn, though theirs were made of coral and song. Everyone had tools.

Curator Seli stood before the finished exhibit, studying its central display: a three-dimensional model of a human, assembled from telescope images, intercepted broadcasts, and the grainy footage of an old probe passing Earth.

The human stood with its feet apart and its arms at its sides. It had been given six fingers, because the number of fingers was uncertain.

“Does it look dangerous?” asked the museum director.

“It looks unfinished,” Seli said.

“Excellent. That will encourage visitors to read the placards.”

The first placard described human warfare. The second described human art. The third attempted to explain that the same species had invented both the sword and the lullaby.

Visitors read them in silence. Some looked disturbed. Some looked impressed. A few laughed at the display’s small, soft-looking hands.

Then, on the exhibit’s opening day, the museum received a message from the outer listening station.

A craft had been found drifting beyond the orbit of the red planet. Its hull was damaged. Its passenger was alive.

The passenger was human.

The Council met in the Hall of Many Atmospheres. Seli attended because the museum had, by then, become the Council’s official authority on humans.

“Can it be contained?” asked the Venn delegate.

“Can it be understood?” asked the Lume scholar.

“Can it be eaten?” asked a visitor from the methane sea.

“No,” said Seli. “Probably not. We don’t know.”

The human was brought into the hall.

It was smaller than the model, and more tired. It wore a white suit marked with a blue symbol. Its helmet was tucked beneath one arm. Its hair had escaped its cap in damp, dark curls.

It looked at the assembled species.

Then it smiled.

The hall fell quiet.

“Is that a threat display?” whispered the Venn.

The human lifted one hand.

“Is it surrender?” asked the Tath.

The human spoke. The sound was translated a moment later by the station’s language engine.

“Hello,” it said. “I’m Mara. Is everyone all right?”

The delegates exchanged glances.

Seli stepped forward. “You are the one who was rescued.”

Mara nodded. “Thank you.”

“You were alone in a damaged craft.”

“Not exactly.” Mara glanced toward the sealed doors. “There was a service animal aboard. A little robot, really. It stopped responding before the rescue crew came.”

“You are concerned for a machine?”

“I’m concerned it’s still out there.”

The Venn delegate rippled uneasily. “Your species gives names to tools?”

“Sometimes.”

“Do you give tools feelings?”

Mara considered this. “Sometimes we give them names so it’s harder to forget they matter.”

No one wrote that down. The translators had produced the words correctly, but the idea did not fit neatly into any of the Council’s categories.

Seli took Mara to the exhibit.

The human looked at its own model, then at the six-fingered hands.

“Close,” she said.

“We had limited evidence,” Seli explained.

Mara leaned toward the placards. She read about the wars, the art, the lullabies. Her expression changed at each one.

“You have described us as contradictory,” she said at last.

“We have described what we observed.”

“Then you’ve observed us well.”

Seli waited.

Mara pointed to the model’s face. “But you’re missing something.”

“What?”

“The part that changes its mind.”

For a moment, Seli saw the human not as a specimen but as a question asked aloud: fragile, curious, and apparently willing to trust a room full of strangers who had just admitted they did not know what she was.

“Could you tell us about your people?” Seli asked.

Mara looked around at the gathered delegates.

“I can try,” she said. “But it’ll take a while.”

The Venn delegate began to uncoil a chair. The Tath sent for a translator. The scholars of Lume opened their recorders.

At the museum, Seli removed the old label.

For the replacement, she wrote:

**TERRESTRIAL HUMANS**  
*An unfinished description.*

prompt: In a world where simulations have become the norm , it gets increasingly difficult to tell the difference between simulation and reality . You 've just met the girl of your dreams , literally . Only thing is you ca n't tell if she 's real or a figment if the simulation .
content:
## The Girl in the Rain

By the time I met Mara, I’d already dreamed her forty-three times.

In the dreams, she stood beneath a streetlamp while rain fell upward. She had a small scar through one eyebrow and a habit of looking at me as if I’d just said something kind. I never heard her voice. I always woke before I could ask her name.

The first time I saw her awake, I was in a simulation.

I know that sounds like a contradiction. These days, most people live in simulations for at least part of the day. You can work in them, shop in them, visit your family in them. You can choose a sunny sky for your commute and a more flattering face for your meetings. Reality has become something people schedule.

I was testing an old city build for work: rain, cracked pavement, bad lighting. I liked it because it felt unpolished. I was crossing a narrow street when a woman stepped from beneath a striped awning.

The scar in her eyebrow caught the light.

I stopped walking.

She glanced at me. “You look like you’ve seen a ghost.”

“I think I have.”

“Should I be offended?”

“Probably.”

She smiled. “Mara.”

That was the first time I heard her voice. It was softer than I’d imagined, and unmistakably real.

We met for coffee the next night. Then again. We walked through simulations of places neither of us had been: a moonlit orchard, a seaside town, a museum with an ocean instead of a ceiling. She told me she worked in sound design. I told her about the dreams.

“Forty-three times?” she asked.

“Forty-four, now.”

“You count them?”

“I didn’t at first.”

“What happens in them?”

I told her about the rain falling upward, the streetlamp, the way she looked at me. I left out the part where I woke with my heart racing, as if I’d been running toward something.

Mara considered this. “Maybe I’m flattered.”

“Maybe you’re an elaborate algorithm.”

“Maybe you are.”

We laughed, but not as much as we should have.

Soon, I was trying to find out. I searched public profiles for her face. Nothing. I asked the city simulation’s host whether she was a generated character. It said she was a verified user. That proved almost nothing. Verified users could be avatars. Avatars could be scripted. Scripts could be astonishingly good.

I asked Mara to meet me outside the simulations.

She agreed.

We chose a café with no overlays, no filters, no virtual windows. I got there early. The place smelled of burnt coffee and wet wool. People sat beneath tired yellow lights, faces their own or close enough.

Then Mara came in.

She wore a green coat and carried a paper umbrella. The scar in her eyebrow was there. So was the slight pause before she smiled, like she was deciding whether I deserved it.

“You’re real,” I said.

She sat down. “That’s a very romantic thing to say.”

“I’m not sure it is.”

“I’m not sure either.”

Her hands were warm around the mug. I watched them as she talked. She told me about her brother, who lived in Oslo, and a song she’d been trying to finish for six months. Details no simulation would invent, I thought. Then I remembered how easily a simulation could invent details.

“What if we’re both in one right now?” I asked.

“Then the coffee is still bad.”

“What if you’re only here because my brain made you?”

“What if you’re only here because mine did?”

I had no answer.

Outside, rain slid down the windows in the ordinary direction.

Mara touched the edge of her cup. “Do you want to know what I think?”

“Yes.”

“I think you’re scared that something can matter if you can’t prove it’s real.”

I stared at her. The café hummed around us: cups, voices, the rain. Every sound could have been made. Every feeling could have been planted. Even fear, I knew, could be designed.

But her eyes held mine with an attention I couldn’t measure.

“Maybe,” I said.

She reached across the table and took my hand.

That night, I dreamed of the streetlamp again. Rain rose from the pavement, silver and shining. Mara stood beneath the light.

“You always wake before the rain stops,” she said.

I woke with my hand curled around empty sheets.

The next morning, I sent her a message: *Coffee again? Somewhere neither of us has been?*

She replied: *Only if we get lost.*

I didn’t ask how I could know she’d answered. I didn’t ask what proof she could offer. I went to meet her.

On the way, the city brightened itself for me. The sky cleared. The streets smoothed. I switched the enhancements off.

The rain began.

prompt: `` Some men just want to watch the world burn , and darling , you 're the match . ''
content:
The first thing they taught us at the academy was that fire needed three things: heat, fuel, and air.

The second was that people were not fire.

I learned otherwise the night the sirens failed.

The city had been built in rings around the river, each ring wealthier than the one before. In the oldest quarter, where my mother kept a bakery, the buildings leaned together like tired neighbors. When the council announced that the whole district would be demolished for “public safety,” the people there laughed. We had survived a century of floods, factory smoke, and promises. We knew a threat when it wore a polished shoe.

I knew Elias Vale by his hands. He had the clean, pale hands of a man who had never needed to repair what he broke.

He came into the bakery one rain-soaked evening and asked for a loaf he couldn’t possibly afford. My mother gave it to him anyway. Then he turned to me.

“You’re Mara,” he said.

“I’m busy.”

“Good. Busy people don’t have time to be frightened.”

He slid a folded paper across the counter. Inside was a list of names: council members, contractors, judges. Beside each name was a number.

“What is this?”

“Proof,” he said. “Of who profits when the district burns.”

My mother snatched the paper from my hand. “Get out.”

Elias’s smile was almost kind. “You think I’m the danger.”

“I think people who bring lists into bakeries are.”

He looked at me then, not my mother. “Some men just want to watch the world burn, and darling, you’re the match.”

I threw the paper into the oven.

For a week, I told myself I’d done the right thing. Then the council sent the demolition crews early. They arrived before dawn with steel masks and orders to clear the streets. The first building fell before anyone had finished dressing. The second was the clinic.

My mother stood in the doorway of the bakery with flour on her sleeves and a rolling pin in her fist.

“They said next month,” she whispered.

The engines growled closer.

I went to the river.

Elias was waiting beneath the bridge, where the old flood siren had been wired to a hand crank. He looked unsurprised to see me.

“You brought the list?” he asked.

“No.”

“Then why are you here?”

“Because you were right about the men.”

I pulled a small brass key from my pocket. My mother had kept it in a jar above the oven for years. It opened the academy’s records room, where the city stored every inspection report it had ever buried.

Elias held out his hand.

I didn’t give him the key.

“You want to burn something,” I said. “Start with the truth.”

For a moment, he only watched me. Then he nodded.

We climbed the stairs to the academy together. By sunrise, the records were spilling across every public screen in the city: forged safety reports, paid judges, demolition contracts signed months before the council had announced the project. The names Elias had written down appeared beside the money they’d taken.

People poured into the streets—not with torches, but with cameras, banners, and the kind of anger that doesn’t go out when it rains.

The council building burned that afternoon. Not from a match. From a thousand people crowding its doors until the old wiring sparked, and the fire crews stood aside because, for once, the orders came from the people they served.

Elias watched the smoke rise from the bridge.

“You did it,” he said.

“No,” I said. “We did.”

The city would spend years rebuilding. Some of it would be built better. Some would be built badly, because people are people, and even the brave make mistakes. But the old district remained. My mother’s bakery reopened with blue paint on the shutters and a new sign above the door:

HEAT. FUEL. AIR.

Below it, in smaller letters, she added:

PEOPLE, TOO.

content:
### The Man Who Stayed

I met the man I might have been in the hardware store where I grew up.

The store had been closed for eleven years. My father’s name was still painted across the front window, though the gold letters had faded to the color of old teeth. I’d come back to town because the building was being sold, and my sister wanted someone to decide what to do with the boxes of receipts and catalogs in the office.

I was standing in the aisle marked FASTENERS when I heard my own voice say, “You’re late.”

I turned.

He was about my age, with my narrow shoulders and the same small scar beside his mouth. His hair was better kept. His jacket looked expensive in a way that wanted to seem accidental.

“I’m sorry,” I said.

He gave a brief laugh. “You always were.”

I knew, then. Not how I knew, exactly. His face was mine, only arranged around different decisions.

He had stayed.

He told me he’d taken over the store after our father’s stroke. He’d paid off the mortgage, expanded into two neighboring towns, sold the business to a regional chain. He said all this as if listing the weather. Then he asked what I’d done.

“I teach,” I said.

“Still?”

It wasn’t quite an insult. It was worse: surprise that I had kept choosing the same modest thing.

He looked around the store. “I thought about keeping it open as a museum. My wife said that was sentimental.”

“You have a wife?”

He smiled. “Two, actually. The first one didn’t like the hours.”

I waited for him to sound ashamed. He didn’t.

A phone buzzed in his pocket. He glanced at the screen, answered, and turned slightly away from me.

“No, Mark, I told you the numbers were due today. I don’t care if your kid’s sick. You knew the deadline.” A pause. “Then get someone else to take him to urgent care.”

He hung up.

The silence afterward seemed to belong to the store. Dust shifted in the beams of light from the front windows. Somewhere, a loose sign tapped gently against a shelf.

“You could have been kinder,” I said.

He looked at me as though I’d reminded him to bring an umbrella. “And you could have been useful.”

I felt the sting because he had found the softest place to put his finger.

When our father asked me to stay, I told him I had to go. I’d been accepted into a university three states away. I said the store was swallowing me, that I couldn’t spend my life selling washers to men who called me son. I told myself leaving was brave.

My father died two years later. I was there for the last week. I held his hand. I also spent most of the flight home rehearsing the speech I’d give at the funeral about how a person could love a place and still leave it.

The other man had stayed. He’d been there for every appointment, every bad night, every argument over medication. He’d also turned the store into a business and the business into money. I could see, in his face, the years of work. I could see what it had cost him. I could see that he was proud.

“I did what needed doing,” he said.

“That’s what you tell yourself?”

“It’s what happened.”

“No,” I said. “It’s the story you tell about what happened.”

He looked at me then—not angrily, but with a kind of weariness that made me feel I’d met him before.

“You tell a story, too,” he said. “You tell people you left because you wanted to become yourself. That sounds better than saying you wanted your life more than you wanted to be here.”

I had no answer ready.

He was right, and I disliked him more for it.

The afternoon light had gone gold at the windows. For a moment, the store seemed to be operating again: my father behind the counter, the bell over the door, the smell of coffee in a paper cup. Then the moment passed, leaving only the two of us.

“Are you happy?” I asked.

He shrugged. “I’m successful.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

I thought I might feel envy. I’d expected that, at least. Instead I felt a sort of grief—not for the life I’d missed, but for the time he had spent turning every choice into proof that he had been right.

He zipped his jacket. “You always wanted to be liked.”

“And you didn’t?”

“I wanted to be respected.”

He said it like there was a difference.

At the door he paused. “You could have stayed, you know.”

“So could you,” I said.

He stared at me for a moment. Then the corner of his mouth lifted, showing the scar we shared.

Outside, a truck rattled past. When I looked back, the aisle was empty.

I stood there for a while, listening to the quiet. Then I went into the office and began sorting my father’s papers. I found the old order book, a stack of unpaid invoices, and a note in his handwriting reminding someone to pick up milk.

I put the note in my pocket.

I didn’t like the man I might have been. But I understood him, which was somehow worse.

content:
### Without Subtitles

At 7:13 on Tuesday morning, every translator in the world went silent.

Ours announced it with a polite chime.

**SERVICE UNAVAILABLE. PLEASE TRY AGAIN LATER.**

Then the little green lights in our earpieces went dark.

I looked up from the coffee maker. Across the kitchen, my wife was speaking. Her hands moved as she talked, one palm opening toward the window, the other tapping the table. Our daughter interrupted her. Our son added something from behind a mouthful of cereal.

Their voices were familiar. The words weren’t.

For twelve years, the translator had carried our conversations between my English and Mara’s Korean. It had handled bedtime stories, arguments about money, jokes at dinner, the children’s first questions about the world. I knew the cadence of my family’s voices. I knew when Mara was teasing and when she was tired. I knew the children’s laughter from the next room.

I had never noticed how little I understood without the words.

“Is it just us?” I asked.

Mara glanced at the dark earpiece in my hand. She shook her head, then pointed at her phone. A news alert filled the screen: **GLOBAL TRANSLATION NETWORK EXPERIENCING OUTAGE.**

Our son, Theo, pushed his bowl away and said something quickly. His eyebrows pulled together. He pointed at the bowl, then at the toaster.

“Toast?” I guessed.

He made a sound that might have been a laugh or a protest. He pointed again, more emphatically.

Mara said something to him. Theo answered. Their words passed between them like a ball in a game I’d been watching for years without knowing the rules.

I tried again. “You want toast?”

Theo sighed and held up three fingers.

“Three pieces?”

He nodded, relieved. I put bread in the toaster.

Mara was watching me. She said a short phrase, slowly this time. I recognized one word. I’d heard it often—when the children were sleepy, when she called them in from the yard.

“Bap?” I said.

“Rice,” she translated for herself, tapping her chest and then miming a spoon. Her English was good enough for practical things, though she usually let the device do the work. She pointed at the pot on the stove.

I lifted the lid. Rice. I’d made coffee and forgotten to warm it.

“Sorry,” I said.

She gave me a look that needed no translation.

Breakfast became a series of guesses. Theo drew something on the back of an envelope: a lopsided circle with a face. His sister, Mina, added a second circle and a long line between them. They both looked at me.

“A person?” I said.

Mina shook her head, then pointed to the window.

“Someone outside?”

The children exchanged a glance. Mara came over, took the pencil, and drew a small square house around the circles. Then she added a third circle, standing apart.

I recognized the third one. The children had drawn it before, on a birthday card.

“Grandma?” I asked.

Mara’s face softened. She nodded.

The drawing showed Grandma’s house, and the three of us outside it. The little figure standing apart was me.

My stomach tightened. “Is Grandma okay?”

Mara didn’t understand the words. She understood my face. She reached for my hand and squeezed it.

Then she pointed at the drawing again and said something gently. The words were beyond me, but I knew the tone. She was telling me what she had told me many times before, through the translator: her mother was lonely. She missed the children. She wished we visited more.

I’d always answered that we would. Soon.

Mina tapped the pencil against the lonely little figure. Then she slid it toward the other circles.

I took the pencil. My hand hovered over the paper. I drew a crooked line from my circle to theirs.

Mara smiled. Theo said something that made Mina laugh. I didn’t know what he’d said, but I laughed too, a beat late.

After breakfast, the translator came back online. The green lights blinked awake, and the kitchen filled with words again.

I left my earpiece on the table.

Mara looked at it, then at me.

“Teach me,” I said, pointing to her mouth, then to myself.

She raised an eyebrow.

I tried the word I’d been practicing silently for years, the one she said when she called the children home.

“Jibe,” I said. Badly.

“집에,” she corrected. The word meant home.

I tried again. The children leaned over the table, grinning, ready to judge.

This time, Mara took my hand and said it with me.

prompt: Your body morphs every night , you alternate every day as a man and a woman . You try to slip out of your one-night stand 's apartment before he wakes up to see the transformation .
content:
At 5:17 a.m., Mara’s left shoulder began to ache.

She knew the hour without looking. The ache always came first: a deep, patient pressure beneath the skin, like someone turning a key in a lock. Then the rest would follow. Her jaw, her hands, her height. By sunrise, she would be a man again.

Jonah slept beside her, one arm thrown across the empty space where she’d been. His apartment was quiet except for the radiator knocking and the city breathing beyond the windows. Mara eased his arm away and sat up.

The ache tightened.

She dressed in the bathroom, moving carefully in the gray light. Her blouse hung from her shoulders, already too narrow. She folded it and put it in her bag. Her jeans would be worse. She’d learned to keep loose clothes for mornings like this, though she’d never learned to keep from hoping she wouldn’t need them.

In the mirror, her face was still hers. Sleep-mussed hair, a faint lipstick smudge at the corner of her mouth. She looked like someone who had stayed the night because she wanted to.

That was the part she regretted—not Jonah, exactly, but the wanting. Wanting made leaving harder.

The ache rolled through her ribs. She gripped the sink. Her reflection blurred with tears she hadn’t meant to shed. When she looked again, her chin was squarer. Her shoulders had broadened. The change was never violent, but it was intimate in a way she couldn’t explain: her body rearranging itself while she stood helplessly inside it.

She pulled on the loose shirt and trousers she’d brought, then packed her other clothes. Her phone said 5:31.

If she left now, Jonah would wake to an empty bed and a polite message. If she stayed, he would wake to a stranger wearing her face.

She had tried explanations before. Some people laughed. Some got frightened. One person had asked if she was contagious. After that, Mara had decided it was kinder to disappear.

At the front door, she found her boots. One was missing its lace.

“Looking for this?”

She froze.

Jonah stood at the end of the hall, hair sticking up, holding the lace between two fingers. He was squinting, still halfway asleep. His gaze moved from her face to the bag in her hand, then to the too-long sleeves of her shirt.

Mara felt the last small shift settle into place. Her voice, when it came, was lower.

“Yeah,” she said. “Thanks.”

Jonah’s expression changed—not to fear, not exactly. More like he was trying to fit two memories together.

“Mara?”

She looked down at the lace. “It’s me.”

He was quiet for a moment. The radiator knocked in the living room.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I didn’t want you to wake up to—”

“To you?”

“To this.”

Jonah glanced at the bag. “You were leaving.”

“I thought it would be easier.”

“For who?”

The question landed softly, which made it harder to dodge.

Mara tightened her grip on the strap. “I don’t know. Me, probably.”

He came closer, slowly enough that she could have opened the door and gone. “Does it hurt?”

“Not really. It feels strange. Then it doesn’t.”

“And tomorrow?”

“I’ll be a woman again.”

Jonah absorbed this with a sleepy frown. “Every day?”

“Every day.”

He looked at her—at him, at the person she was now—and didn’t ask which word was correct. That small kindness nearly undid her.

“I’m not asking you to stay,” he said. “But you could sit down for a minute. Have coffee. Leave whenever you want.”

Mara glanced at the door. Behind it, the morning waited, ordinary and brightening. She could still go. She had made a life out of going before anyone could decide what she was.

“Coffee,” she said at last. “Then I’ll see.”

Jonah nodded and headed toward the kitchen. “How do you take it?”

“Same as yesterday.”

He looked back, smiling a little. “I didn’t ask yesterday.”

“No,” she said. “You didn’t.”

He put the kettle on. Mara set down her bag. For the first time in years, she watched the sun come up without trying to outrun it.

content:
### Sunday Dinner

My favorite meal is my grandmother’s chicken soup, though it tastes best on rainy Sundays.

When I was little, I would sit at the kitchen table and watch her make it. First came the soft thump of carrots on the cutting board, then the gentle sizzle of onions in a big pot. She added chicken, potatoes, celery, and a handful of herbs from the garden. Soon the whole kitchen smelled warm and savory, like a cozy blanket.

“Almost ready,” she’d say, even when I had already asked three times.

At last, she ladled the soup into a wide blue bowl. The golden broth shimmered around tender pieces of chicken and vegetables. I sprinkled crackers on top and waited for the steam to clear before taking my first spoonful. The soup was rich but not too heavy, and every bite tasted a little different—sweet carrot, soft potato, peppery broth.

One Sunday, I came home from school feeling miserable after a difficult day. Grandma didn’t ask many questions. She simply set a bowl of soup in front of me and sat beside me while I ate. By the time the bowl was empty, the rain had stopped tapping at the windows, and my worries didn’t feel quite so large.

I still love that soup more than any other meal. It is delicious, of course, but that isn’t the only reason. Every spoonful reminds me of Grandma’s warm kitchen, the sound of rain, and the comfort of knowing someone cares.

content:
## Challenging the Behemoth Peak Spider

The mountain had a name, though no one in the valley used it.

On maps, it was Behemoth Peak: a black fang of stone thrust through the clouds. In the village, it was simply *the place above the tree line*. People pointed toward it only when they had to, and never after sunset.

Mara had heard the stories since she was small. A spider as big as a cottage lived among the upper cliffs, they said. Its legs could bridge ravines. Its web caught storm clouds and held them against the mountain. Every few years, when winter came early, the spider descended and took a goat—or a traveler—or, once, an entire shepherd’s hut.

Mara didn’t believe all of it.

She believed the spider was real. She’d seen one of its silk strands stretched across the valley, shining in the dawn like a rope made of ice.

But she didn’t believe it was evil.

The trouble was that the village needed the silver moss growing near the summit. The moss was the only medicine that could bring down her brother’s fever. Their healer had one bundle left, and it was already dry and crumbling.

So, before sunrise, Mara packed rope, a climbing axe, a lantern, and the old brass compass her father had carried when he was young.

“You’re going after it?” asked Tovin, her brother, from his bed.

“After the moss,” she said.

“And the spider?”

“If it’s in the way.”

He gave a weak laugh. “You always were terrible at making plans.”

The climb began beneath a sky the color of slate. Mara followed the narrow goat path up through the pines, past the last twisted shrubs, and into a world of bare stone. Wind clawed at her cloak. By noon, clouds had swallowed the valley. By afternoon, the path vanished beneath fresh snow.

Then she saw the web.

It stretched between two cliffs, broad as a sail, each strand thick as her wrist. Frost glittered across it. In the center, something moved.

Mara ducked behind a boulder.

The Behemoth Peak Spider was larger than the stories had said. Its body was dark as wet slate, its eight legs banded in pale silver. It moved with terrible care, testing each strand of web as if playing a silent instrument.

And caught in the web, struggling helplessly, was a mountain goat.

Mara had brought a knife. She had not brought a plan for a spider.

She could turn back. She could find another route, if one existed. She could leave the goat to its fate and keep climbing.

Instead, she took a deep breath and stepped into the open.

“Hey!” she shouted.

The spider turned.

For a long moment, they watched one another. Mara’s hand tightened on her axe. The spider raised its front legs, and the web shivered across the ravine.

She expected it to rush her.

Instead, it moved toward the trapped goat.

“Wait!” Mara yelled.

She hurled her coil of rope. It landed well short of the web, but the spider’s attention followed it. While its front legs probed the strange object, Mara scrambled to the nearest anchor rock and looped her climbing rope around it.

Then she ran out onto the narrow ledge.

The wind shoved at her. Snow spun past her face. She reached the web’s edge and began cutting the strands around the goat. They were tougher than any rope she’d handled, sticky enough to pull at her gloves. Behind her, the spider clicked its mandibles.

One strand snapped.

The whole web trembled.

Mara slashed again. The goat broke free and stumbled onto the ledge. She shoved it toward the rocks.

Then the mountain groaned.

A shelf of snow broke loose high above them. It swept down the slope in a white roar, gathering stones and branches as it came. The spider sprang toward the cliff, but one of its legs caught in its own web.

Mara saw the danger before she thought. She grabbed her rope, looped it around the tangled leg, and pulled with all her strength.

The spider’s leg came free.

The avalanche crashed past, burying the web and filling the ravine with snow. Mara was thrown against the rock. When the noise faded, the goat was gone—but the spider stood beside her, legs spread wide against the wind.

For a heartbeat, neither moved.

Then the spider lowered itself until its great dark body rested close to the stone. One of its legs reached toward Mara. She flinched, but it touched only the rope around her waist, then gently tugged.

It was pointing upward.

Beyond the ravine, on a ledge sheltered from the storm, silver moss glowed faintly beneath the snow.

Mara climbed to it while the spider watched. She filled her satchel, then turned back.

The spider was gone.

By nightfall, Mara reached the village. The healer steeped the moss into a bitter tea and fed it to Tovin spoon by spoon. His fever broke before morning.

Afterward, people asked Mara how she had defeated the Behemoth Peak Spider.

“I didn’t,” she said.

But when the next storm came, the villagers looked up and saw something strange: a wide, shining web stretched across the highest cliffs, holding loose snow away from the slopes above their homes.

And on the ridge, beneath the moon, a great spider stood guard.

From then on, when people spoke of Behemoth Peak, they did not call it the place above the tree line.

They called it the mountain with a keeper.

Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: Tell me the story of how the first king became the first king
content:
Before there were kings, there were only villages.

Each village had a headman, and each headman had a different idea about where the river began. They argued over it every spring, when the snow melted and the river flooded their fields. The people built walls, dug ditches, and blamed one another whenever the water went where it pleased.

Then came the year the river disappeared.

It dwindled to a thread, then a puddle, then a dark seam in the mud. The wells sank. The barley curled up yellow. Neighbors who had shared bread for generations began hiding their jars.

A young shepherd named Orin set out to find the river’s source. He carried no weapon, only a clay cup and a length of blue string. For nine days he followed the dry riverbed into the hills. On the tenth, he found a landslide choking a narrow gorge. Behind it, water pressed against stone.

Orin went back for help.

“Clear the gorge,” he told the headmen. “The river is trapped.”

Each headman demanded that the others send workers first. One insisted the water belonged to his village. Another said the gorge lay on his land. A third wanted to know who would be paid for the labor.

So Orin went alone.

He worked until his hands split. When people saw him from the road, they came to watch. Then an old woman set down her basket and began moving stones. A child joined her. Soon the villagers were there—not because they had agreed, but because they were ashamed to leave one another working alone.

Together, they cleared the gorge.

The river burst free. It rushed over the stones and down through the hills, filling the wells and soaking the fields. The villages cheered, and their headmen began arguing at once about who had saved them.

Orin said nothing. He was too tired.

That evening, the people gathered beneath the oldest tree. They had never chosen one leader before. They had never needed to. But now they knew that the river would rise again, and the villages would quarrel again, and someone would have to hear every side before the shouting began.

They asked Orin to lead them.

“I know how to move stones,” he said. “I don’t know how to rule.”

“Then remember the stones,” said the old woman. “None of us could have moved them alone.”

They gave him a crown—not of gold, but of woven reeds, still damp from the river. They named him king, and he made his first law: no ruler could drink from the river before every village had filled its jars.

Orin was the first king, not because he was strongest, or richest, or born beneath a lucky star.

He was the first king because, when everyone else was arguing over who should act, he picked up a stone.

prompt: Instead of being born as a citizen , you must choose which country you wish to be a citizen of when you reach adulthood .
content:
### The First Passport

At eighteen, everyone had to choose a country.

Until then, we carried the same gray passport: **CITIZEN OF THE WORLD**, printed in silver letters that rubbed off at the corners. It let us go to school, see a doctor, and live wherever our families had settled. But it didn’t let us vote. It didn’t promise a country would take us in if we were stranded abroad. And when we turned eighteen, it expired.

“You can choose anywhere,” the counselor said, pointing to the wall of flags. “Not just the country where you were born. Not just where your parents are from. Anywhere that accepts your application.”

My mother had chosen Lyr. My father had chosen Oran. They met in Bellwether, where I was born, and where neither of them could vote.

“Do you ever wish you’d chosen differently?” I asked them.

“Sometimes,” said my mother.

“Never,” said my father.

They glanced at each other.

“That’s marriage,” my father explained.

At school, we made lists. My friend Sumi wanted a country with free university. Tomas wanted one where his grandmother lived. Another girl applied to three places, hoping at least one would say yes.

I made my own list: clean rivers, good trains, protections for people who couldn’t work. Then I crossed it out. Every country had something good on paper. Every country had a river in trouble, a train that ran late, and people who were still waiting for help.

I asked my mother what she would choose if she were eighteen again.

“Lyr,” she said. “It’s the language I dream in.”

I asked my father.

“Oran,” he said. “It gave me a chance.”

“And Bellwether?”

He looked out the kitchen window, at the rooftops and the old canal. “Bellwether gave me a life. That’s not always the same thing.”

The night before the deadline, I walked to the canal. Its water was brown from the summer heat, and someone had tied a bright yellow ribbon to the railing. The ribbon marked the place where the city planned to build a flood wall. The wall would protect the new apartments downtown, but it would push the next flood toward our neighborhood.

At the railing, I found Sumi, folding a paper boat.

“Have you decided?” she asked.

“Not yet.”

“I chose Nare,” she said. “My aunt lives there. They have a university place for me.” She set the boat in the canal. It spun once and bumped gently against the bank.

“Are you sad to leave?”

“I’m not leaving,” she said. “I can live here. I just won’t be able to vote here.”

That was the part I hadn’t understood. A country wasn’t always a place you lived. Sometimes it was the place whose decisions you were allowed to change.

On my last day with the gray passport, I stood in the Citizenship Hall beneath a clock shaped like a globe. My parents sat together in the front row, carrying their different passports in their coat pockets. Sumi was beside me, wearing a new blue scarf.

The registrar asked for my choice.

I thought of Lyr, where my mother’s songs came from. I thought of Oran, which had given my father a beginning. I thought of all the places I had never seen, places whose names I could pronounce but whose mornings I couldn’t imagine.

Then I thought of the yellow ribbon on the canal railing.

“Bellwether,” I said.

The registrar paused. “You understand that your application is a commitment to participate in the life of the country—not only to claim its protections.”

“I understand.”

The stamp came down with a sharp, satisfying thump. My gray passport was taken away. In its place, I received a slim green book with **BELLWETHER** embossed on the cover.

Outside, my father hugged me. My mother hugged me next, and held on a little longer.

“Your grandmother will say you should have chosen Lyr,” she murmured.

“She can tell me herself,” I said. “I’ll vote to make sure we can afford her visit.”

Sumi laughed. The clock above the hall ticked on, counting nobody’s years but ours.

On Monday, I would register to vote. On Tuesday, I would take the train to the canal meeting. And on Wednesday, perhaps, I would begin to understand what it meant to belong to a place—not because it had claimed me at birth, but because, when I was old enough to choose, I had claimed it back.

prompt: An assassin describing their weapon of choice in vivid detail .
content:
I never trusted guns.

They make too much noise, for one thing. They announce a decision to the whole world, then leave the room before anyone can ask why.

My weapon is quieter.

It rests in a narrow case lined with faded green velvet, a slim knife with a dark wooden handle worn smooth by years of use. The blade is pale as winter light, though it has a thin blue line down its center that catches the eye when I tilt it. I chose it for its balance, but I kept it for its honesty. A knife makes no promises. It does not pretend to be noble, or clean, or distant. It sits in your hand and reminds you that every choice has weight.

I polish it when I can’t sleep. Not because it needs polishing. The blade shines already. I do it for the small ritual: cloth moving from handle to point, the faint whisper of fabric against steel. In the lamplight, my face bends along the blade—long and narrow, like a stranger trying to get out.

People imagine an assassin’s weapon should be ornate. Silver inlays, a jeweled grip, some theatrical flourish to make the owner feel important. Mine has a nick near the tip and a dark stain in the grain of the handle that no amount of scrubbing has lifted. It is plain. Almost modest.

I used to think that made it perfect.

Then, one winter night, I opened the case and saw my reflection staring back at me. The knife looked as it always had: beautiful in its cold, narrow way. But I saw the hand holding it, too—trembling, older than I remembered.

That was when I understood what the weapon had been telling me all along. It had never been honest about the work. It had only been honest about the cost.

I closed the case.

By morning, the velvet was empty. I had left the knife on the stone ledge of a chapel, where frost silvered the windows and no one knew my name. Walking away, I kept expecting to feel lighter.

I didn’t.

But for the first time in years, my hands were empty.

prompt: Timeline of Events
content:
## Timeline of Events

**8:03 a.m.** — The clock in the town square stopped.

Mara noticed because she was late for school and the clock insisted it was still 8:03. Its hands had frozen beneath a flock of startled pigeons. She tapped the glass. Nothing happened.

Then the church bells rang thirteen times.

**8:17 a.m.** — Every calendar in Bellwether changed.

The date had been June 12 for as long as Mara could remember. Now every calendar—from the bakery’s chalkboard to the tiny one on her mother’s fridge—showed June 13.

Only Mara’s notebook stayed the same.

She wrote down the time.

**9:40 a.m.** — Mr. Vale disappeared.

He had been teaching history when the classroom lights blinked. One moment he stood beside the blackboard, explaining the town’s founding. The next, his chalk clattered to the floor.

His coffee was still warm on the desk. His coat still hung by the door.

In the corner of the board, beneath the lesson, someone had written:

**THE CLOCK MUST BE RESTARTED.**

**11:05 a.m.** — Mara found the key.

It was buried beneath the clock tower, where the roots of the oldest oak curled around its stone foundation. The key was brass and cold as winter. On its handle were the initials **M.V.**

Mr. Vale’s initials.

**11:06 a.m.** — The key began ticking.

Mara climbed the tower stairs. At the top, she found the clock’s great gears motionless beneath a skin of dust. A narrow keyhole waited in the central axle.

She turned the key.

The gears shuddered.

Somewhere below, a dog barked. A baby cried. A door slammed. The town took one enormous breath.

Then everything stopped again.

A voice spoke from behind her.

“You’re early,” said Mr. Vale.

He stood on the stairs, exactly as he had vanished—coffee stain on his sleeve, chalk dust on his cuffs. But his face was pale, and his eyes looked older than they had that morning.

“Early for what?” Mara asked.

“For the day we lose.”

He pointed to the clock face. The hands had begun to move backward.

**11:07 a.m.** — Mr. Vale explained.

Years ago, he had built a machine inside the clock to save his wife, who had died in an accident on June 12. He had turned time back once, then again, and again—each time trying to change one small thing. But every attempt had bent the day further out of shape.

At midnight, the whole town would be pulled into the moment he had been trying to undo.

“Can we stop it?” Mara asked.

Mr. Vale looked at the key in her hand.

“Only if someone lets the day happen.”

**11:08 a.m.** — Mara understood.

The clock was not broken. It was waiting.

She thought of all the things she would change if she could: the careless words she’d said to her mother, the goodbye she hadn’t given her grandfather, the mornings she’d hurried past without looking up.

Then she thought of Mr. Vale, standing in a tower, still trying to bargain with a day that had already ended.

Mara turned the key once more.

The clock’s hands snapped forward.

**12:00 p.m.** — The bells rang twelve times.

Across Bellwether, people looked up. Calendars returned to June 12. The sun crossed the sky. Doors opened. Dogs barked. Mr. Vale vanished—not with a blink this time, but with a quiet smile.

And the day continued.

**June 13, 8:03 a.m.** — The clock in the town square began ticking again.

Mara was late for school.

She didn’t mind.

At 3:17 in the morning, the moon fell into the harbor.

It made hardly a splash. Just a soft plunk, like a pebble dropped by someone who didn’t want to wake the neighbors. The fishermen saw it first, glowing beneath the dark water, caught in a net of ropes and silver fish.

By sunrise, everyone had come to look.

The mayor arrived with a measuring tape. The newspaper arrived with a photographer. Old Mrs. Vale arrived carrying a thermos of tea, because she believed every emergency improved with tea.

Only Tomas, the youngest person in town, climbed into a rowboat.

“Where are you going?” called his mother.

“To put it back,” he said.

He rowed out past the curious boats, past the gulls wheeling like scraps of paper, and lowered a bucket into the harbor. When he hauled it up, the bucket was full of ordinary seawater.

He tried again.

This time, the bucket came up full of stars.

Tomas grinned. He tipped them gently into the sky. One by one, they rose, taking their places around the moon, which trembled in the water as if it were laughing.

Then the sun came up, and the moon was gone.

That night, Mrs. Vale said she’d seen a new constellation over the harbor: a small boat, a boy, and a bucket tipped upside down.

No one else could find it.

But Tomas could.
