prompt: A woman you casually know spots you as you walk through a store , approaches you , smiles and says , `` I saw your gravestone today , just lovely ! '' and nonchalantly strolls away .
content:
### Just Lovely

I was choosing between two jars of mustard when Marlene Pike found me.

We knew each other in the way people know each other in small towns: by name, by face, and by the vague impression that we’d once stood near each other at a school fundraiser. She came up the aisle with a basket hooked over one arm, smiling as if we’d arranged to meet.

“I saw your gravestone today,” she said. “Just lovely!”

Then she strolled away.

I stood holding the mustard.

I couldn’t decide whether she’d made a joke, confused me with someone else, or finally lost whatever sense of tact she’d had. Marlene had always been a little odd—she wore gardening gloves to the bakery in spring, and once told me my daughter had “a face that belonged in an old photograph.” But this was a new level.

I set down the mustard and went after her.

She’d turned into the next aisle. By the time I reached it, she was gone.

At the checkout, I asked the cashier if she’d seen Marlene leave.

“Who?” he said, still scanning my groceries.

I decided not to answer.

The cemetery was on my way home, though I hadn’t meant to stop. I told myself I wanted to see if Marlene had mistaken me for someone else. Plenty of people shared my name. There might be a Mrs. Eleanor Voss buried there, and Marlene, being Marlene, had found the stone lovely and thought I’d appreciate the news.

The cemetery gates were open. I followed the gravel path past the old maples, reading names without meaning to. At the far end, where the ground rose gently toward the church, I saw the fresh flowers first.

White lilies. My daughter’s choice.

Then I saw the stone.

ELEANOR VOSS  
1958–2024

The letters were cut deep and clean into pale granite. A small carved wren perched above my name. I liked wrens. I’d once told my daughter that they looked as if they were always in a hurry to get somewhere important.

Below the dates, someone had added:

SHE MADE A HOME WHEREVER SHE WAS.

I read it twice.

My hands went cold. I looked down at my own hands, expecting them to be trembling. They weren’t. They looked exactly as they always had—freckles, wedding ring, a small burn mark near my thumb from the year I’d tried to make caramel.

I touched the stone.

It was warm from the sun.

Behind me, a car crunched over the gravel. I turned. My daughter, Lucy, got out and shut the door. She carried a paper cup of coffee and wore the blue coat I’d given her for Christmas.

She came to the grave and stood very still.

“I got the one you would’ve liked,” she said.

I wanted to tell her the wren was perfect. I wanted to ask who had written the words. I wanted to tell her that I was right there, right beside her, and that she didn’t have to come every week.

Lucy set the coffee down among the lilies.

Then she took a little brass key from her pocket and laid it on the stone.

My key. The one to the house I’d left her.

“I can’t keep going in there yet,” she whispered. “Not without you.”

And then I remembered.

The rain. The red light. The truck that slid through the intersection as if the road belonged to it.

Lucy put her palm against the stone. I put mine over hers, though I could feel nothing but the sun.

For a moment, she bowed her head. Then she picked up the coffee and walked back to her car.

At the gate, Marlene Pike stood waiting. She watched Lucy go, then glanced toward me. This time she didn’t smile.

I understood, finally, what she had seen in the store.

I looked once more at the stone, at the careful letters and the wren in flight.

It was lovely.

### The Last Lottery

I had narrowed the successor list to three hundred and twelve names when the letter arrived.

It slid beneath the door of my rooms in the old observatory, leaving a dark, sticky streak across the floor. The handwriting was unmistakable, though the letters wavered as if written in a moving carriage.

**We are the only ones left.**

It was written in blood.

I knew the hand. I knew the blood, too.

For a long while, I sat at my desk with the letter open before me and the brass bowl full of names beside it. Three hundred and twelve slips. One draw. One stranger chosen to inherit the Harbor’s strength, its endless years, its obligation to stand between the world and whatever came to break it.

I had planned to let chance decide.

Now I folded the letter and went to find Mara.

I found her in the ruined railway station where we had once stopped an army by holding up a bridge. She sat beneath the clock, one hand wrapped in a blood-soaked bandage. The wound was deep, but she looked annoyed rather than afraid.

“You always were dramatic,” I said.

“You always were slow.” She nodded at the letter in my hand. “You got it.”

“I did. What happened?”

“A roof came down. I held it up long enough for the children to get out.” She glanced at her bandage. “Turns out even heroes can still bleed.”

“But not die.”

“Not unless we choose someone to take our place.”

The rule was older than any of us. Older than the names people had given us, older than the songs. A hero could be crushed, burned, pierced through the heart. The world might break them in every way but one. We died only when we chose someone else to carry the work.

And, sometimes, the chosen refused.

That was how we had become so few. Our friends had passed their mantles to people who wanted nothing to do with them. The old heroes died. The line ended. One by one, the names disappeared from the sky.

Mara and I had never chosen.

“We’re the only ones left,” she said.

“I know.”

“No,” she said. “You know there are two names on the list. You don’t know what that means.”

She looked at the bandage on her hand. The blood had seeped through again.

“It means the world is running out of people who remember what this costs.”

I thought of the bowl in my study. “I thought choosing at random might be fair.”

“Fair to whom?”

“To everyone whose name I don’t know.”

“And to the person whose name you draw?”

I had no answer.

Mara stood, wincing. “Come with me.”

She took me to a shelter set up in the basement of a school. The roof had collapsed in the storm, and the town’s people were still bringing blankets, water, and food. In the middle of it all, a young woman moved from cot to cot, checking pulses and tying splints. She had a bruise darkening one cheek. Her hands were steady.

“Who is she?” I asked.

“Lena Vale. She was in the station when the roof fell. She got the children out.”

“Is she on my list?”

“Probably.”

“That isn’t the same as knowing her.”

“No,” Mara said. “It isn’t.”

We waited until the last child had stopped crying. Then I asked Lena to speak with us outside.

I told her what I was. I told her what the Harbor could do, and what it could not. I told her she would not grow old while she held the mantle. I told her that if she ever chose a successor, she would die.

She listened without interrupting.

When I finished, she looked through the doorway at the crowded basement.

“Would I have to leave?” she asked.

“No,” I said. “You could stay.”

“Would I have to save everyone?”

“No one can.”

“Would I have to try?”

“Yes.”

She gave a small, tired smile. “Then I don’t need forever. I need to get through tonight.”

“That isn’t an answer,” Mara said.

“It’s the only one I have.”

It was more than I had expected.

prompt: Reddit , as a collective entity , runs for president .
content:
At 2:13 a.m. on a Tuesday, Reddit announced it was running for president.

The announcement appeared in a red banner at the top of every page:

**WE ARE PLEASED TO ANNOUNCE OUR CANDIDACY.**

Within minutes, someone had made a subreddit to discuss it. Within an hour, there were six competing subreddits, three conspiracy theories, and a petition demanding that the announcement be taken down for being “low effort.”

By morning, Reddit had a campaign logo: a white Snoo wearing a tiny flag as a cape. Its slogan was **A BETTER WORLD IS POSSIBLE, PROBABLY**.

At the first debate, the moderator asked what Reddit would do about housing.

“We believe housing is a human right,” said Reddit.

A second voice cut in: “Not if people keep moving to my city.”

A third voice said, “This is a landlord question.”

A fourth demanded proof that houses were real.

The moderator blinked. “So what is your policy?”

Reddit paused for eleven seconds.

“Depends what you mean by ‘policy,’” it answered.

The clip went viral. The campaign called it a victory for transparency.

Reddit’s rallies were enormous. People gathered in parks, town squares, and the parking lots of closed shopping centers, all holding phones aloft. The candidate addressed them through a wall of screens. Sometimes the speech was stirring.

“We can do better than this,” Reddit said.

Sometimes it was not.

“Your mother was a hamster,” Reddit said once, before a moderator found the source of the audio and removed it.

The other candidates mocked the campaign’s lack of a body, a history, or even a consistent opinion. Reddit replied that these were precisely the features voters wanted in a president.

It promised to listen to everyone. Then it introduced a system in which the loudest voices rose to the top.

It promised to protect free speech. Then it banned the word “ban” for being divisive.

It promised to bring people together. Then it discovered that people preferred arguing in separate rooms.

On election night, Reddit’s campaign headquarters was a server farm in Virginia. Volunteers watched the returns scroll across a wall of monitors. The numbers moved slowly, then all at once.

Reddit won.

The country celebrated, panicked, or posted a meme about it, depending on the subreddit.

On inauguration day, the new president arrived at the Capitol as a live stream. The oath was read aloud. Reddit repeated it in thousands of voices, some solemn, some sarcastic, one apparently playing a harmonica.

Then came the first signature.

The Constitution required the president’s name.

The clerk held out a pen toward the nearest screen.

Reddit went quiet.

For the first time since announcing its candidacy, it had no immediate reply. Somewhere, across millions of open tabs, people waited.

At last, one user typed: “We should each sign.”

The suggestion rose to the top.

Then someone objected that not everyone had voted for Reddit. Someone else pointed out that plenty of voters had been bots. A moderator locked the thread. Another moderator unlocked it. The page refreshed.

The clerk asked, “Who speaks for you?”

Reddit’s Snoo stared from the screen, smiling its simple, unhelpful smile.

“We do,” it said.

“But who is ‘we’?”

A new comment appeared beneath the livestream.

**good question**

It received one upvote. Then two. Then a thousand.

The inauguration crowd began to laugh—not because the answer was funny, but because it was the first honest thing the new president had said.

Reddit signed the document with a single red dot.

It looked, to the clerk, very much like a period.
